articles.text:
HASI: $500 Million Green Notes Offering To Support Renewable Energy And Sustainable Infrastructure Investments
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 9:47 AM
HASI: $500 Million Green Notes Offering To Support Renewable Energy And Sustainable Infrastructure Investments
HA Sustainable Infrastructure Capital (HASI) has priced a $500 million registered public offering of green junior subordinated notes bearing an interest rate of 7.850% and maturing in 2057. The financing will support the company’s sustainable infrastructure investment strategy, including projects involving renewable energy, storage, and energy efficiency.
The offering was priced on November 9, 2026, with settlement expected on November 24, subject to customary closing conditions.
HASI estimates that net proceeds will total approximately $493.3 million after underwriting discounts and other offering expenses.
The notes will be guaranteed on a subordinated basis by several affiliated entities.
These include Hannon Armstrong Sustainable Infrastructure, Hannon Armstrong Capital, and certain related holding companies.
Junior subordinated notes generally rank below senior indebtedness in the order of claims against a borrower.
The structure provides HASI with long-term financing while establishing the specific priority of the securities relative to other obligations.
HASI intends to use the immediate proceeds to temporarily repay portions of existing borrowings.
These may include obligations under its Standalone Commercial Paper Program, unsecured credit facility, and Credit-Enhanced Commercial Paper Program.
The company will allocate an amount of cash equal to the offering’s net proceeds toward acquiring, investing in, or refinancing eligible green projects.
Projects may include those with qualifying disbursements made during the 12 months preceding the issuance date.
The company may also allocate funds toward eligible projects with disbursements expected within two years following issuance.
Before the full amount has been allocated to qualifying investments, HASI may retain funds in short-term interest-bearing instruments or apply them toward temporary debt repayment.
This structure is intended to provide flexibility in managing the financing while maintaining a commitment to eligible sustainable infrastructure investments.
HASI invests across multiple categories of energy transition infrastructure.
Its portfolio includes utility-scale solar projects, onshore wind generation, energy storage, distributed solar and battery systems, renewable natural gas, and energy efficiency.
The company manages more than $19 billion in assets.
Its investment strategy combines financing expertise with long-term relationships involving energy developers and infrastructure operators.
Renewable energy and storage projects can require substantial upfront capital before generating recurring revenue.
Infrastructure investors provide financing through debt, equity, and structured capital arrangements to support these developments.
HASI’s business focuses on deploying capital into projects that offer financial returns alongside measurable environmental benefits.
The latest green notes offering provides additional financial resources for these activities.
It also expands the company’s long-term financing through securities scheduled to mature in 2057.

Torus, a Salt Lake City energy infrastructure manufacturer, launched Foundry, a prefabricated modular AI compute system, and raised $500 million in growth capital led by Magnetar on Nov. 11. Participating investors include ICONIQ, Origin Ventures, Ridgeline Partners and Trinity Capital.
Foundry packages power, storage, cooling, networking and compute into a single modular unit that installs at existing commercial and industrial sites in 12 to 16 weeks, a fraction of the multiyear timeline typical for a hyperscale data center campus. Each site delivers 1 to 20 megawatts of capacity, with the smallest unit roughly the size of a cargo van. The system taps spare grid capacity that utilities have already allocated to existing sites, avoiding the infrastructure upgrades that often trigger rate increases.
The raise follows a $200 million investment from Magnetar in September 2025 , making this the second nine-figure investment the Evanston, Illinois-based asset manager has made in Torus in just over a year.
Betting on inference over training
The launch targets a shift in AI economics: Data center demand for inference, the process of running trained models rather than building them, is projected to grow at a 35% compound annual rate through 2030, compared with 22% for training, according to McKinsey . Unlike training, inference runs continuously and benefits from sitting close to users, pulling demand toward smaller, distributed sites rather than centralized campuses.
“Most providers are bringing power to the chips. Foundry brings the chips to power,” says Nate Walkingshaw, founder and CEO of Torus, who previously served as chief experience officer at Pluralsight before founding Torus in 2021.
“One of the biggest challenges in scaling AI infrastructure is access to power, and the solution isn’t simply generating more of it, but making better use of what’s already available,” says Dave Snyderman, managing partner and global head of alternative credit and fixed income at Magnetar. “Torus has spent years building the energy infrastructure and expertise to address this challenge. Foundry builds on that foundation by bringing compute to available power, helping unlock capacity within the existing grid.”
Photo courtesy of Torus
Foundry ships in three configurations: a powered shell without GPUs, a turnkey bare-metal unit with GPUs included, and a single-tenant sovereign model for enterprises that want exclusive hardware. Torus launched the product with its first customers, bare-metal GPU cloud provider Hydra Host and an unnamed AI cloud provider, and plans to have more than 47,000 GPUs running in Foundry units by the end of 2027.

articles.title: SoftBank-Led Agile Robots Raises $500M Series F at $8.5B Valuation
articles.snippet: SoftBank-Led Agile Robots Raises $500M Series F at $8.5B Valuation Wowtale
articles.text:
A German company that has deployed more than 20,000 industrial robot solutions now has a plant that can build up to 10,000 humanoids a year. Munich-based Physical AI company Agile Robots has raised a $500 million Series F led by SoftBank Group, valuing it at $8.5 billion and bringing total funding to $2 billion.
Agile Robots announced the round on Nov. 12. SoftBank Group led, with NVIDIA, Hitachi Group (Hitachi and Hitachi Ventures) and T.Capital among the participants. The company says the investors span the automotive, artificial intelligence, digital and industrial technology sectors. SoftBank is a longtime backer: its Vision Fund 2 led the company’s $220 million Series C in September 2021 at a valuation above $1 billion, so the new valuation is more than eight times that. According to Bloomberg, a round of about $800 million, with SoftBank anchoring more than $300 million, was under discussion in June, and the round closed smaller at $500 million. Hitachi Ventures also joined Graphon Labs’ $35 million Series A this month.
The company builds humanoid and mobile robots, robotic arms and hands, and the software and AI models behind them, aimed at automotive, consumer electronics, healthcare and service customers that want to automate tasks that have relied on human dexterity and judgment. It was founded in 2018 as a spin-off from the German Aerospace Center (DLR) and says it has deployed 20,000 industrial robotic solutions across automotive, consumer electronics, logistics and other industries. It has more than 3,500 employees from almost 60 countries, including more than 2,000 R&D experts, and over 650 patents, and develops and builds its hardware and software in-house from more than 20,000 square meters of lab space.
Founder and CEO Zhaopeng Chen said the company wants to bring Physical AI out of the lab and into industrial production across logistics, automotive, electronics and manufacturing. The money will go to global expansion, a stronger presence in key markets and more production capacity. Agile Robots plans to strengthen its presence in the United States and speed up development of new robotics applications, while continuing to build out production capacity, including in Germany. A new site opened early this year in Fürstenfeldbruck, near Munich, can produce up to 10,000 legged and wheeled humanoid robots a year. Dennis Chang, managing partner at SoftBank Investment Advisers, said Agile Robots combines deep robotics expertise with the ability to execute at industrial scale, and that SoftBank looks forward to continuing to partner with Chen’s team.
Acquisitions have widened the business. In November 2023 it took over the operations of insolvent Munich robotics company Franka Emika , which now runs as Franka Robotics and serves as an AI robotics research platform. Last November it announced the acquisition of thyssenkrupp’s Automation Engineering business , and in April it closed the deal . The unit now operates as industrial deployment specialist Krause Automation, and the company said at the time it would add about 650 experts and 10 locations in Europe and North America. BÄR Automation and Idealworks are also subsidiaries, and its humanoid lineup includes Agile ONE. The company has not disclosed revenue.

Agile Robots Raises $500 Million From SoftBank and Nvidia

While Europe is still debating whether humanoid robots will ever make it onto the factory floor, SoftBank and Nvidia are putting half a billion dollars on the table for it: Agile Robots, the Munich-based robotics company, has just closed a funding round of $500 million (about €450 million). The round lifts its valuation to $8.5 billion (about €7.6 billion), the German news agency dpa reported.
The Round at a Glance
Hard Facts
Agile Robots
Valuation

about $2 billion (about €1.8 billion)
Existing investors
including SoftBank Vision Fund and Xiaomi
SoftBank is not a new backer: The Japanese company already led the $220 million Series C in 2021 that made Agile Robots a unicorn. How much SoftBank is contributing this time is not known. The other names are no surprise, either. Nvidia had already announced its investment in Agile Robots in Berlin in October, and the company has been working since September on physical A.I. for manufacturing with Hitachi, which is investing through its venture arm. T.Capital is the investment company of Deutsche Telekom.
What the Money Is For
Zhaopeng Chen, the founder and chief executive, wants to use the capital mainly for three things: entering the U.S. market, new industrial applications and manufacturing in Bavaria. Early this year, Agile Robots opened a new plant in Fürstenfeldbruck, near Munich, that is designed for up to 10,000 humanoid robots a year. The company is taking the technology straight from the lab into industrial series production, Mr. Chen said.
According to The New York Times , the round is also meant to prepare for a possible initial public offering. There is no timetable for that. Physical A.I. could help Europe close its gap with the United States and China in artificial intelligence, Mr. Chen argued there.
What Agile Robots Does
Agile Robots was started in 2018 as a spinoff of the German Aerospace Center, known as DLR, in Oberpfaffenhofen. Mr. Chen had worked there on, among other things, especially sensitive robot hands. Today the company sells almost everything that moves in a factory: robot arms, robot hands and grippers, driverless transport systems, complete production cells and the humanoid robot Agile ONE, along with its own control platform.
By its own account, Agile Robots employs more than 3,500 people at more than 25 sites, over 2,000 of them in development. More than 20,000 automation solutions are installed worldwide, it says, and it holds more than 650 patents. Its customers include large companies in the automotive, consumer electronics, health care and logistics industries.
Agile Robots has also grown through acquisitions, including that of Franka Robotics, a Munich maker of robot arms. For A.I., the company relies on partners: A research partnership with Google DeepMind has been running since the spring, followed in October by a humanoid platform based on Nvidia’s robotics models and a logistics project with Audi. Besides Germany, the company also manufactures in China and India, and its earlier investors include Xiaomi, the Chinese electronics company.

Agile Robots Hits $8.5bn Valuation as SoftBank and NVIDIA Back $500m Funding Round
The Munich-based robotics company Agile Robots has secured $500 million in fresh funding, putting it among Europe’s most highly valued private robotics businesses as investors look beyond generative AI towards industrial automation.
Munich, 15 November 2026 – Agile Robots , the German Physical AI company, has raised $500 million in a Series F funding round at a valuation of $8.5 billion , according to an announcement issued on 12 November.
Led by SoftBank Group, the round attracted investment from NVIDIA, Hitachi Group – including Hitachi and Hitachi Ventures – and T.Capital, among others. It brings the Munich-based company’s total funding raised to $2 billion.
The investment comes as the artificial intelligence industry increasingly turns its attention to machines capable of performing physical tasks. For Agile Robots, the challenge is no longer simply developing intelligent robotics technology, but producing and deploying it economically at industrial scale.
Agile Robots Funding: Key Facts
Company: Agile Robots
Headquarters: Munich, Germany
Founded: 2018
Funding round: Series F
Capital raised: $500 million
Company valuation: $8.5 billion
Total funding raised: $2 billion
Lead investor: SoftBank Group
Other investors: NVIDIA, Hitachi Group and T.Capital
Industry: Physical AI, robotics and industrial automation
Global deployments: More than 20,000 industrial robotic solutions, according to the company
Expansion plans: United States, Germany and additional international markets
Funding announcement: 12 November 2026
From Artificial Intelligence to Physical AI
Founded in 2018 as a spin-off from the German Aerospace Center (DLR), Agile Robots develops robotic systems that combine artificial intelligence, sensors and precision engineering.
Its products range from industrial robotic arms and dexterous hands to mobile and humanoid robots, supported by proprietary software and AI models.
The distinction between conventional automation and Physical AI is commercially significant. Traditional industrial robots generally perform predefined tasks in structured environments. AI-enabled systems aim to interpret changing conditions and adapt their behaviour accordingly.
That could open up more complex activities in manufacturing, logistics and electronics assembly, where tasks have historically depended on human dexterity and judgement.
Yet technical capability alone will not determine adoption. Manufacturers must be convinced that these systems can operate safely, reliably and at a cost that justifies replacing or supplementing existing processes.

SoftBank’s decision to lead the latest funding round, alongside NVIDIA’s participation, puts Agile Robots in the spotlight as investors seek commercial applications for artificial intelligence beyond software.
The new capital will finance international expansion, further robotics development and additional manufacturing capacity.

articles.title: Agile Robots raises $500 million led by SoftBank
articles.snippet: Agile Robots raises $500 million led by SoftBank CASRAI
articles.text:
Munich-based Agile Robots announced on November 12, 2026 that it had closed a $500 million Series F led by SoftBank Group, with NVIDIA among the participants. The financing supports international expansion and manufacturing, putting fresh capital behind a robotics business whose research connections include Franka Robotics and a Google DeepMind partnership. Reuters confirmed the announcement .
A $500 million round for expansion and production
The round values Agile Robots at $8.5 billion and takes its total funding to $2 billion. Alongside SoftBank and NVIDIA, participants include Hitachi Group, comprising Hitachi and Hitachi Ventures, and T.Capital. The company’s November 12 announcement says the proceeds will support a larger presence in the United States, additional production capacity including in Germany, and entry into new markets.
Founder and chief executive Zhaopeng Chen described the financing as a way to accelerate expansion and bring intelligent robots into industrial production. SoftBank Investment Advisers managing partner Dennis Chang said Agile combines robotics expertise with industrial execution, adding: “We believe Physical AI will transform industries.” These are the company’s and investor’s expectations for the business.
Tech.eu’s November 12 report places the investment in an existing industrial operation: Agile’s machines assemble products, handle components, inspect equipment and move materials through factories. Its portfolio extends across robotic arms, hands, autonomous mobile robots and humanoids, together with their software and AI models.
Factory capacity and installed systems measure different things
Reuters reported that Agile opened its Fürstenfeldbruck factory, near Munich, earlier in 2026. The company says it can produce up to 10,000 legged and wheeled humanoid robots annually. That is a stated capacity ceiling, rather than a report of annual output or shipments.
Separately, Agile reports more than 20,000 robotic solutions installed worldwide. Its announcement describes deployments across automotive, consumer electronics, logistics and other industries; it does not identify that total as humanoid installations. Treating the two numbers as interchangeable would obscure the difference between the company’s established industrial business and its humanoid manufacturing ambitions.
The financing release also gives no allocation of the proceeds between the United States, German production and other markets. It therefore establishes the expansion priorities without quantifying how much additional capacity each location will receive.
A research spin-off with an academic hardware connection
Agile was founded in 2018 as a spin-off from the German Aerospace Center, according to Reuters and Tech.eu. The company reports more than 2,000 research and development specialists and over 650 patents. Its path from a public research institution into industrial automation provides a concrete technology transfer connection for universities following the investment.
There is also a direct research equipment link. Franka Robotics says it has belonged to Agile Robots since 2023. Franka describes its Research 3 system as a force-sensitive platform for robotics and AI, giving researchers low-level access to robot control and learning capabilities. Its website also says Agile’s Diana 7 now supports the Franka Control Interface, extending the ecosystem to a robot with greater reach and payload capacity.

By: Asia Business Outlook Team | Thursday, 12 November 2026
Japanese investment group SoftBank has led a US$500 million funding round in German robotics company Agile Robots , valuing the company at US$8.5 billion.
The funding round also saw participation from semiconductor company Nvidia , Japanese technology firm Hitachi and T. Capital.
The investment comes as interest in artificial intelligence and robotics continues to grow, with more companies looking to use these technologies in manufacturing and other industries.
Agile Robots plans to use the funds to expand its business in the United States, increase production in Germany and develop new industrial applications.
The company is looking to benefit from the growing demand for automation technology across manufacturing, logistics and other sectors. The investment is also expected to help it strengthen its position in the global robotics market .
Key Highlights
SoftBank Leads $500 Million Funding Round in German Robotics Firm Agile Robots
Agile Robots Reaches $8.5 Billion Valuation After SoftBank-Led Investment
Nvidia and Hitachi Join SoftBank in $500 Million Investment in Agile Robots
SoftBank and Nvidia Support Agile Robots' Expansion
Founded in 2018 by researchers from the German Aerospace Center, Agile Robots develops robotic systems that combine artificial intelligence with advanced hardware. Its products include industrial robotic arms , robotic hands, autonomous transport systems and humanoid robots used for different industrial applications.
The company has more than 3,500 employees across over 25 locations worldwide. It also says that more than 20,000 of its automation solutions are currently in use globally. Agile Robots holds over 650 patents related to its technology.
With the latest investment, the company has raised approximately US$2 billion since its establishment. SoftBank had previously led a US$220 million Series C funding round in Agile Robots in 2021, helping it expand its operations.
Nvidia's participation is another important part of the deal. The chipmaker has been increasing its investments and partnerships in robotics as it looks to expand the use of AI beyond computers and data centres. This includes physical AI , which allows machines to understand their surroundings and carry out tasks in the real world.
Agile Robots has also partnered with Google DeepMind to improve the capabilities of its robotic systems. The collaboration is aimed at developing robots that can perform more complex tasks in industrial settings.
Company Plans to Increase Production in Germany
Agile Robots will use the new funding to expand its operations in the United States and increase its manufacturing capacity in Germany. It also plans to develop more applications for its robotic systems as manufacturers look for ways to improve productivity and reduce manual work.
Earlier this year, the company opened a manufacturing facility in Fürstenfeldbruck, near Munich. The facility is designed to produce up to 10,000 humanoid robots annually. This will help Agile Robots increase production and prepare for growing demand.

Germany’s Agile Robots Raises $500M in Series F Funding to Expand Physical AI Production
By Greg Bock · 12 November 2026 · 2 min read
Insider Brief
German robotics company Agile Robots raised $500 million in Series F funding at an $8.5 billion valuation to expand physical AI production capacity and strengthen its international operations.
The SoftBank Group-led round included Nvidia, Hitachi Group and T.Capital, bringing Agile Robots’ total invested capital to $2 billion.
Agile Robots reports 20,000 deployed industrial robotic solutions and operates a German facility capable of producing up to 10,000 legged and wheeled humanoid robots annually.
German robotics company Agile Robots has raised $500 million in Series F funding at an $8.5 billion valuation to increase manufacturing capacity and expand its physical AI business internationally.
The SoftBank Group -led round included Nvidia , Hitachi Group, through Hitachi and Hitachi Ventures , and T.Capital . According to Agile Robots , the financing brings its total invested capital to $2 billion.
The Munich-based company plans to use the funding to strengthen its presence in the United States, expand production capacity, including in Germany , and develop additional robotics applications.
Agile Robots makes humanoid and mobile robots , robotic arms and hands , along with the AI models and software used to control them. Its customers include companies in the automotive, consumer electronics, healthcare and service industries.
“Physical AI will fundamentally change how the world builds, moves and makes things,” founder and CEO . Zhaopeng Chen said. “Our vision is intelligent robots working alongside people in factories and warehouses everywhere, and Agile Robots is determined to lead that shift. We bring Physical AI out of the lab and into industrial production, across logistics, automotive, electronics and manufacturing.”
Expanding Industrial Production
The company reported that it has deployed 20,000 industrial robotic solutions since its founding, including systems used in automotive manufacturing, consumer electronics and logistics. Earlier this year, Agile Robots opened a manufacturing facility in Fürstenfeldbruck, near Munich, with the capacity to produce up to 10,000 legged and wheeled humanoid robots annually.
Agile Robots was founded in 2018 as a spin-off from the German Aerospace Center (DLR), initially focusing on bringing robotics research into industrial applications.
The company now has more than 2,000 research and development specialists and over 650 patents, according to the announcement. Its portfolio includes Franka Robotics, an AI robotics research platform, and Krause Automation, an industrial deployment specialist recently acquired from thyssenkrupp.

Peak 10 Energy: $500 Million Facility To Finance Oil And Gas Acquisitions
By Amit Chowdhry
Today at 11:14 AM
Peak 10 Energy: $500 Million Facility To Finance Oil And Gas Acquisitions
Peak 10 Energy has established a financing partnership with U.S. Bank that provides as much as $500 million for acquisitions of producing oil and gas assets across the U.S.
The acquisition finance facility will support Peak 10’s strategy of consolidating packages weighted toward proved developed producing properties. These assets have established production and can generate more predictable cash flows than undeveloped acreage.
U.S. Bank structured the facility to support later asset-backed securities issuances. That approach could provide longer-term institutional financing after Peak 10 completes and assembles acquisitions.
Peak 10 was founded in 2023 and has completed 12 acquisition and divestiture transactions involving operated properties, non-operated interests, and mineral assets across U.S. onshore basins.
The new facility will allow the company to pursue larger transactions and close acquisitions more quickly. Peak 10 said it encountered additional opportunities during 2026 that it could have acquired if the facility had already been available.
The company also maintains a commodity hedging relationship with U.S. Bank. Hedging can help stabilize cash flow from acquired properties and support financing by reducing exposure to oil and gas price volatility.
Peak 10’s strategy focuses on extending the productive lives of existing fields and infrastructure. The company expects this approach to support domestic energy production without depending solely on new exploration.
Legacy Star Capital Partners backs Peak 10 and views the combination of producing-asset consolidation and asset-backed financing as a long-duration investment strategy.
Petrie Partners originated the transaction and advised Peak 10. Baker Botts served as Peak 10’s legal adviser, while Haynes Boone represented U.S. Bank.
KEY QUOTES
“This facility and our commodity hedging relationship with U.S. Bank give us the financial firepower to close acquisitions at a scale that matches the opportunity we see in the market.”
Kyle McQuire, Chief Executive Officer of Peak 10 Energy
“The ABS structure provides a durable source of capital, and reflects the practical, solutions-oriented approach our structured lending team brings to help clients achieve their objectives.”
William Eustis, Co-Head of Asset-Backed Securities at U.S. Bank
